352ced96796d8926: From Azam Mohd
The 2027 budget raises a question Malaysians rarely ask: who bears responsibility when national promises reach citizens unevenly? The answer cannot rest with Putrajaya alone.

A budget becomes meaningful through state governments, local councils, schools, clinics and businesses. Malaysians should therefore judge this spending plan by whether public institutions can work together across administrative boundaries.

Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim tabled a RM460 billion federal budget on Oct 9. The finance ministry projects growth of 4.2% to 5.2% next year, while the fiscal deficit is expected to narrow to 3.3% of gross domestic product.
These forecasts are not guarantees. Their significance depends on what happens after Parliament approves expenditure and ministries begin implementation.
Consider the distance between a federal announcement and a household’s experience.

A parent may welcome education funding but still be confronted with an overcrowded classroom. A patient may hear about health allocations yet encounter long waiting times. A trader may qualify for financing but struggle with permits, infrastructure or inconsistent local enforcement.
Getting things done
None of these difficulties can be resolved by increasing appropriations alone. The missing ingredient is coordination.

Federal ministries design programmes, states control land decisions, and local authorities shape everyday business conditions. When their priorities diverge, public money can purchase activity without producing improvement.

The resulting frustration is often blamed entirely on whichever party governs nationally, although responsibility may be distributed across several institutions. This is particularly important for Sabah and Sarawak, where distance, infrastructure gaps and administrative arrangements complicate delivery. The same principle applies to rural districts in Peninsular Malaysia and densely populated urban neighbourhoods.

Equal allocations do not necessarily create equal access. A credible federal budget must recognise different costs and starting conditions without turning regional needs into partisan bargaining chips.

The 2027 budget also arrives amid uncertainty surrounding the Middle East conflict. Bank Negara Malaysia has announced additional financing support for smaller enterprises facing temporary cash flow pressures. Such measures can help firms survive disruption, but credit cannot repair a blocked supply route or eliminate higher transport costs. Businesses need agencies responsible for financing, logistics and trade facilitation to respond coherently together.
Delivering on promises

Malaysia, therefore, needs a delivery compact between federal and state institutions. For major programmes, the responsible ministry should identify the implementing agencies, milestones and obstacles. State governments should disclose the approvals and infrastructure commitments under their control. Local authorities should report service bottlenecks.
These arrangements would make responsibility visible without assigning every problem one political owner.

Parliament has an important role. Budget debates too often concentrate on announcements and partisan comparisons. Parliamentary committees should instead examine why comparable districts achieve different results with similar resources. Auditors can test whether procurement and implementation follow established rules, while elected representatives can question delays without alleging misconduct.
Poor performance warrants investigation; it is not, by itself, proof of corruption.

There are legitimate objections. Reporting can become bureaucratic, and states may resist federal conditions that intrude upon their constitutional responsibilities. The solution is not another elaborate national dashboard. It is a limited set of jointly agreed service standards, published responsibilities and independent verification, designed around programmes where fragmented authority obstructs delivery.
Out of the political fray

Political competition makes this more urgent. With the next general election approaching, governing parties will claim achievements while opponents highlight shortcomings. Both have legitimate democratic roles.

But citizens should be able to distinguish a policy that failed because of flawed design from one delayed by procurement, staffing, local approvals or unexpected external shocks. That distinction improves accountability rather than shielding ministers from criticism.

A useful starting point would be to select several high impact programmes spanning education, healthcare, small business support and regional connectivity. Publish who is responsible for each stage, invite state participation and review outcomes after implementation begins.
Where cooperation fails, disclose the disagreement and its consequences. Where it succeeds, retain the practice regardless of which coalition controls the relevant government.
The 2027 budget will ultimately reveal whether Malaysia can move beyond a culture in which announcing expenditure is treated as governing.

The country does not lack ambitious public promises. It needs institutions capable of delivering them together, especially when political loyalties differ. Fiscal credibility begins with sound numbers, but public confidence grows when responsibility is shared, visible and impossible to evade.
Azam Mohd is an FMT reader.

23be0a5665a7f0e9: Dunia ini umpama sebuah penjara yang besar dan dipenuhi dengan segala macam hantu. Itu agaknya yang cuba disampaikan oleh Joko Anwar melalui filem arahannya, Ghost in the Cell. Saya tidak tahu apa genre paling tepat untuk filem ini. Komedi seram absurd barangkali tetapi dalam komedi ada serius dan misteri, ada keganasan, ada aksi ala kartun. Semuanya bercampur, mencetuskan kecelaruan. Joko mungkin mahu menyatakan yang hidup ini beginilah, penuh dengan kecelaruan ragam dan identiti. Malah ada babak yang mengarut sehingga saya teringat filem Kung Fu Hustle arahan Stephen Chow.

Filem Ghost in the Cell ini turut menampilkan dua nama dari Malaysia, Bront Palarae yang memegang watak Jefry, seorang pegawai penjara dan Ho Yuhang sebagai Rendra, seorang banduan yang merupakan ketua sindiket dadah. Ho yang lebih dikenali sebagai pengarah filem membawakan watak penjenayah bertubuh kecil tetapi cukup digeruni.

Cerita bermula dengan Dimas (Endy Arfian), seorang wartawan yang dituduh membunuh ketuanya lalu dihumban ke penjara Labuhan Angsana. Di situ dia bertemu pelbagai jenis manusia, termasuk Anggoro (Abimana Aryasatya), seorang banduan yang sering membela orang lain walaupun tindakannya menyebabkan hukuman penjaranya bertambah. Watak Anggoro memperlihatkan satu paradoks. Dia memang pesalah di sisi undang-undang tetapi masih mempunyai rasa kemanusiaan yang tinggi. Sebaliknya, ketua penjara yang diberikan kuasa menjaga undang-undang pula bersifat binatang atau hantu dalam mengejar pangkat dan kedudukan.

Di penjara itu juga ada Tokek (Aming), banduan ganas yang menjadikan keganasan seksual sebagai alat menakutkan orang lain. Dimas yang baru masuk penjara menjadi sasarannya. Tokek mewakili manusia buas dan gemar membuli orang yang lebih lemah. Melihatkan wajahnya sahaja sudah cukup membuat kita menggeletar. Bagaimanapun, dia mati akhirnya setelah gagal mempertahankan diri apabila berhadapan dengan hantu yang ternyata lebih perkasa. Tokek adalah gambaran manusia yang sebenarnya tidaklah kuat mana tetapi hanya berani kerana dia tahu pihak yang dibuli itu sudah sememangnya penakut. Dia memanipulasi keadaan.

Apa yang menarik perhatian saya ialah cara hantu dalam filem ini membunuh mangsanya. Mayat mangsa disusun dan digubah seakan sebuah arca seni. Ini bagai satu metafora yang menarik. Ia tentang kita yang kadangkala menggambarkan keindahan dengan mempergunakan penderitaan orang lain. Arca memanglah cantik dan hebat tetapi ia dibuat menggunakan mayat yang penuh darah dengan isi perut yang terburai, biji mata terkeluar dan sendi yang patah. Manusia begitulah, mempergunakan hidup pihak lain demi mencari keuntungan dengan menjual gossip dan fitnah, hiburan atau berita buruk tentang mereka. Dan kita gembira menikmati keindahannya sebagai bahan tontonan tanpa mempedulikan kesengsaraan di sebaliknya.

Lebih menarik lagi dalam Ghost in the Cell ini ialah hantu yang membunuh itu akan menyerupai mangsanya sendiri ketika menyerang. Ia seolah-olah manusia itu akhirnya dibunuh oleh kejahatan yang terpelihara di dalam tubuhnya sendiri. Hantu bukan datang dari luar, tetapi dari dalam kita sendiri.

Satu lagi watak yang menarik ialah Six (Yoga Pratama), banduan yang tidak berpegang kepada agama tetapi mempunyai kebolehan melihat hantu dan aura manusia. Ini satu lagi paradoks. Selalunya orang alim yang lebih memahami perkara ghaib. Tetapi dalam filem ini, orang yang tidak beragama pula mampu melihat sesuatu yang gagal dilihat oleh orang lain. Saya melihatnya sebagai sindiran, kerana manusia tak kira apa bangsa atau agama pun tetap dikurniakan tuhan dengan kelebihan masing-masing tetapi adakalanya kelebihan yang diberikan itu tidak mampu difahami olehnya sendiri dan dia perlukan bimbingan. Maka itu, banduan alim bernama Wildan (Mike Lucock) diperlukan untuk mentafsir warna-warna aura yang dilihat oleh Six. Wildan tak mampu melihat aura yang keluar dari tubuh manusia seperti mana Six, tetapi dia mempunyai keilmuan untuk mentafsirkannya. Nah! Begitulah tahap manusia dalam memahami, mempercayai dan menghayati sesuatu. Faham, percaya dan menghayati adalah tiga perkara yang cukup besar bezanya.

Di dalam filem ini, tertarik kepada manusia yang mempunyai aura negatif seperti kemarahan dan kebencian. Untuk mengelakkan diri daripada menjadi mangsa, banduan perlu menenangkan fikiran dan mengawal emosi. Ada yang memilih untuk bersembahyang, ada pula yang menari. Sembahyang merupakan ritual yang menghubungkan manusia dengan tuhan, sedangkan menari lazimnya dianggap kegiatan hiburan. Tetapi dalam filem ini, kedua-duanya boleh menghasilkan ketenangan yang diperlukan untuk menghindari hantu. Yang hendak diperlihatkan bukanlah soal cara mana lebih suci atau lebih baik, tetapi bagaimana manusia mencari ketenangan melalui jalan yang berbeza. Maknanya, ketenangan hati itu penting biarpun kita berbeza pegangan. Tetapi di dalam dunia yang bernama penjara, mereka terpaksa mencari apa saja persamaan untuk terus hidup dengan selamat. Untuk selamat, manusia perlu tenang.

Kemudian kita diperkenalkan kepada Prakasa Kitabuming (Arswendy Bening Swara), seorang politikus dan ahli perniagaan berpengaruh yang menjalani hukuman penjara tetapi masih menikmati kemewahan. Dalam penjara yang sama, ada orang yang hidup berhimpit dan terdedah kepada keganasan, sedangkan orang tertentu masih boleh menikmati layanan istimewa. Sepatutnya apabila seseorang dihukum, pangkat dan kedudukannya tidak lagi memberikan keistimewaan. Orang biasa masuk penjara kehilangan kebebasan. Orang berpengaruh masuk penjara masih boleh bermewah-mewahan. Ada pula watak Sapto sebagai Ketua Penjara yang mempunyai cita-cita besar menjadi Menteri sehingga sanggup tersengih-sengih dan melutut demi membodek Prakasa, politikus yang menjadi penghuni penjaranya sendiri.

Sebenarnya hantu itu mahu mencari Prakasa. Hantu mengikut Dimas ketika Dimas meninjau kawasan hutan Kalimantan yang musnah angkara Prakasa. Tetapi, dalam usaha memburu Prakasa ramai yang menjadi korban. Prakasa menemui ajalnya dengan cukup sinis. Dia berhadapan dengan hantu yang menyerupai dirinya ketika muda, ketika dia konon masih seorang pejuang yang mempunyai cita-cita dan prinsip. Dia adalah gambaran pejuang muda yang telah mengkhianati prinsip perjuangannya setelah berada di puncak kuasa. Hantu yang membunuhnya adalah diri mudanya sendiri yang pernah berapi-api berjuang. Rupanya si pejuang ini telah menjadi tawanan kepada pangkat dan kuasa.

Ada satu babak, kita diperlihatkan dengan sekumpulan banduan artis dan selebriti yang diasingkan daripada kumpulan Dimas dan Anggoro. Dialog lucunya ialah ‘rakyat Indonesia lebih mengambil berat nasib artis daripada nasibnya sendiri'. Saya ketawa kerana sindiran itu bukan masalah di Indonesia sahaja. Kita di sini pun sama. Kita boleh bergaduh siapa betul siapa salah bila artis bercerai dan berantak, kita sanggup masukkan duit di dalam akaun bank pempengaruh media sosial yang mengadu perniagaannya bakal melingkup kerana hutang yang membebankan sedangkan apabila sepupu kita hendak menjual dodol buatannya sendiri, kita tak jawab WhatsApp dia langsung. Kita simpati kepada artis yang sedang sakit tetapi jiran sebelah sudah sebulan terlantar di wad, kita tak jenguk pun. Memang kita semua obses dengan artis dan selebriti.

Joko melihat penjara bukan sekadar set penggambaran dan premis penceritaan. Ia adalah dunia. Dunia boleh jadi syurga jika semua manusianya tenang dan damai tetapi dunia boleh jadi sebuah kurungan yang menakutkan jika di dalamnya bercampur antara manusia baik dengan manusia durjana. Di dalam filem ini digambarkan manusia ada yang mahu berkuasa, ada yang mahu dilindungi, ada yang mahu dipuja dan ada yang sekadar mahu terus hidup. Hantu adalah dosa silam yang memburu manusia itu sendiri untuk menghukum jika manusia tersebut masih tidak mahu berubah menjadi insan yang baik. Di tengah-tengah seram, ngeri, takut dan cemas itu kita masih ada ruang untuk ketawa. Sepertinya kita faham bahawa dunia ini hanyalah senda-gurau sementara sahaja.

Memang semenjak dua ini saya sering menulis tentang filem dan teater yang saya tonton. Ini kerana apa yang ingin saya sampaikan dalam tulisan berkenaan kehidupan telah berjaya dipersembahkan oleh mereka dalam bentuk visual. Saya tidak pastilah tafsiran saya menepati apa yang dimaksudkan oleh karyawan asalnya tetapi inilah yang boleh saya kutip untuk dikongsi bersama. Untuk kita renungi kehidupan ini melalui sebuah persembahan kreatif.

Sebuah karya yang sudah dipertontonkan kepada masyarakat tidak semestinya mempunyai satu tafsiran yang wajib dipatuhi. Kita bebas menterjemahnya. Apa yang saya lihat dalam filem ini adalah tentang perangai manusia yang terpenjara akibat menjadi mangsa kepada nafsu buas sendiri. Nafsu manusia memang tak pernah puas. Jika ada peluang untuk naik, manusia akan naik walaupun akan menindas manusia lain. Dari situlah wujudnya dendam dan pembalasan oleh pihak yang teraniaya. Hantu dalam Ghost in the Cell itu muncul pun kerana manusialah yang mengundangnya. Telah kita pelajari di dalam kitab al-Quran, manusia adalah sebaik-baik kejadian dan makhluk terbaik ini jugalah yang sedang menghancur-musnahkan dunia.

d4e994a42990ef49: From Moaz Nair

The ghost of Malay politics past continues to haunt a fading Umno. Ever since its historic, humiliating downfall in the 2018 general election, the party has been trapped in a state of pathetic paralysis, desperately daydreaming about reclaiming its crown as the nation's undisputed political hegemon.

Yet, instead of executing a clear strategy, Umno's leadership is caught in a dilemma of cowardly choices: suck up to Pakatan Harapan in a volatile unity government, or venture into the wilderness alone, or crawl back to its treacherous former rival PAS.

This delusional "two-tier approach" – trying to play both sides by cutting different deals at the state and federal levels – is a weak political gimmick that has failed to fool anyone, least of all PAS.

Meanwhile, Umno’s relationship with PH has rapidly soured under its current leadership. By even flirting with PAS, a party that relentlessly trashes PH as secular and liberal, Umno is actively incinerating whatever fragile trust it has left with its current governing partners.
Let’s call a spade a spade: this is a desperate, toxic battle for survival.

After bloating itself on power for nearly six decades, Umno still blindly demands to be treated as the "Big Brother" of Malay politics. But wake up: PAS now holds the actual cards. Armed with a superior parliamentary seat count and total control over four state governments -- Kelantan, Terengganu, Kedah and Perlis -- PAS has effectively usurped the throne.
Walking into a trap

Analysts see right through Umno’s terror. The party knows that any formal alliance with the Islamic juggernaut will reduce Umno to the position of a weak, castrated junior partner. History has proven time and again that when these two egos clash over who commands Malay politics, a bloody political knife-fight is virtually guaranteed.
Besides, how short is Umno's memory?

The catastrophic collapse of the 2019 Muafakat Nasional pact should have been a permanent lesson. PAS didn't hesitate to stab Umno in the back, secretly conspiring with Bersatu to form Perikatan Nasional in 2020. Umno president Ahmad Zahid Hamidi openly branded that move a betrayal, and the party rank and file still rightly whisper that PAS carries a "DNA of betrayal".
To walk back into that trap is pure political suicide.

Any attempt at a reunion faces brutal realities: PAS will never surrender the safe, Malay-majority seats it currently locks down. It will greedily force Umno to run in highly volatile, hostile areas, guaranteeing an electoral wipeout of Umno's remaining footprint.

PAS’s aggressive youth wing and top leaders are no longer hiding their ambitions: they want a PAS prime minister. They will never yield the top job to a diminished Umno, shattering any illusion of an equal partnership.
Can Umno survive?

Umno’s traditional lifeline has always been its ability to bridge gaps using non-Malay votes. Crawling into bed with an uncompromising Islamist party will permanently alienate those voters, severing Umno's last remaining oxygen supply.

This desperate anxiety is already reeking at the state level. In Perak and Pahang, Umno leaders hold the posts of menteri besar only out of sheer charity by PH, not because Umno commands a real majority. Inviting PAS into these states is code for a hostile takeover. PAS will effortlessly leverage its momentum, hijack the state machinery, and relegate Umno to political irrelevance on its own turf.

PAS knows it doesn't need Umno; its most realistic path to absolute power remains firmly rooted in consolidating its Malay-Islamic framework. This leaves Umno stranded at a historic crossroads of its own making. Going solo in today’s fractured landscape offers zero guarantee of survival, yet leaping back into the arms of PAS ensures complete subordination to a green wave that has already captured the Malay-Muslim electorate.

If Umno wants to survive, it needs to snap out of its historical delusion. It can no longer demand the "Big Brother" crown based on past glory. It must adapt to a brutal new reality or get comfortable being buried in the footnotes of Malaysian history.
Moaz Nair is an FMT reader.

d4cc7aabe8176b8f: For decades, South Asia was locked in a perpetual cycle of conflict management: brief military clashes between India and Pakistan would be followed by de-escalation and the resumption of formal peace talks, which eventually gave way to another bout of conflict. But this pattern has now been broken.

No high-level dialogue has taken place since 2016. Rather than some temporary diplomatic tantrum, this reflects a paradigm shift in Indian foreign policy, permanently altering the subcontinent’s security architecture.

The roots of this stalemate can be found in the structural failures of past diplomacy. In 1947, 1965, and 1971, Pakistan initiated conventional wars, none of which delivered the results it desired. The third resulted in the breakup of the country and the birth of independent Bangladesh.

These experiences, together with the success of the US-backed mujahideen in their fight against Soviet forces in Afghanistan in the late 1980s, prompted Pakistan’s military to embrace a new strategy, based on asymmetrical warfare—or, more bluntly, terrorism.
From 1989 to 1993, as terrorist attacks caused significant civilian casualties in India, Pakistani officers crowed about “bleeding India to death by a thousand cuts”.
Indian leaders were nonetheless convinced that structured dialogue could persuade Pakistan to abandon this strategy. This belief gave rise to the Composite Dialogue framework in the late 1990s.
This bureaucratic mechanism was designed to segment contentious issues—ranging from Kashmir to trade and humanitarian concerns—so that friction in one area would not derail progress in others.
There was just one problem: every major Indian peace overture was met with an act of military or terrorist provocation that the Pakistani government was either unable or unwilling to prevent.

In 1999, when then-Indian prime minister Atal Bihari Vajpayee undertook his historic bus journey to Lahore to sign a landmark peace declaration, Pakistani troops were infiltrating the Kargil district of Ladakh—actions that led to the Kargil War (which Pakistan lost).

In 2008, when back-channel diplomacy was on the brink of delivering a non-territorial solution to the Kashmir issue, coordinated terrorist attacks by Pakistan-based militants killed 166 innocent civilians in Mumbai.

This cycle exposed a profound institutional disconnect within Pakistan. Its civilian governments lacked the authority or longevity to fulfill the commitments they made at the negotiating table, and its military-intelligence apparatus viewed peace with India as an existential threat to its domestic hegemony.

Now, India has had enough. Prime Minister Narendra Modi initially followed the old peacemaking script. He invited his Pakistani counterpart, Nawaz Sharif, to his 2014 inauguration, and visited Lahore the following year.
Even when this visit was followed by a terrorist attack on the Indian airbase in Pathankot, Modi invited Sharif to join the official investigation into the incident.
Then came the final straw: Pakistan’s joint investigation team concluded that the attack was a “drama staged by India to malign Pakistan”.

With that, India abandoned its doctrine of strategic restraint in favour of a new guiding dictum: talks and terror cannot coexist. India would return to the negotiating table only after Pakistan dismantled, comprehensively and verifiably, its state-supported terrorist networks.

This diplomatic shift was accompanied by a fundamental change in India’s military doctrine. For nearly three decades, Pakistan assumed that its tactical nuclear arsenal would deter India from launching conventional military reprisals for terrorist attacks. Then India decided to call Pakistan’s bluff—most notably, in last year’s “Operation Sindoor”.

Through calibrated retaliatory actions, ranging from surgical cross-border strikes to sophisticated aerial bombardments targeting terrorist infrastructure deep within Pakistani territory, India demonstrated a willingness to accept escalation risks to impose tangible costs on its neighbour.
By signalling that state-sponsored terror would automatically trigger a conventional military response, India has sought to rewrite the rules of deterrence in South Asia.
The current stalemate is hardly desirable. The absence of a diplomatic safety valve between nuclear-armed neighbours poses acute risks to regional, even global, stability.

Even the most basic bilateral matters, such as humanitarian issues, trade blockades, and water sharing, are now viewed through a hyper-politicised national-security lens. And if a new crisis erupts, what mechanism is available to manage it? The margin for miscalculation is perilously thin.

But the prospects for a diplomatic breakthrough remain bleak. Pakistan’s military leadership still pins its domestic political legitimacy partly on hostility towards India, even as the country faces profound economic distress. And India, with its growing economic and conventional-military advantages, has little reason to compromise on its core security interests.

The US is certainly not encouraging India to rethink this stance. Not only has Donald Trump’s administration all but abandoned America’s Indo-Pacific strategy, in which India played a central role as a critical counterweight to a rising China, it has also embraced Pakistan, which, despite its financial instability and close ties with China, has managed to woo the US administration by striking a lucrative cryptocurrency deal with a Trump-linked firm and unctuously nominating Trump for a Nobel Peace Prize.

With the underpinnings of the India-Pakistan conflict firmly entrenched, the current stalemate should be viewed not as a pause between rounds of negotiation, but rather as part of a deliberate strategy of disengagement.

Until Pakistan undergoes a political transformation that fundamentally alters its security calculus, or a “black swan” event forces an existential realignment of regional priorities, the silence across the subcontinent will endure—and the risk of catastrophic error will remain.

Shashi Tharoor, a former UN under-secretary-general and former Indian minister of state for external affairs and human resource development, is a fourth-term elected MP for the opposition Indian National Congress.

a862bb5fa635cfe9: Microsoft took down the Exchange Admin Center (EAC) today after a code change left administrators facing an "Internal Server Error" when trying to access the service. Microsoft first admitted that something was amiss at 0937 UTC on October 12, noting, "When attempting to access the Exchange admin center, affected admins may encounter an 'Internal Server Error' message." Any administrator attempting to access the EAC could be affected. It was more than an hour before the company stated: "We've identified unexpected 302 redirect errors during affected Exchange admin center (EAC) access attempts and are analyzing diagnostic logs to isolate the source of the access failures. "While we continue our investigation, admins remain unable to access the EAC, with no workaround currently available." So, a fun morning for Microsoft's European users. According to Microsoft, the EAC is "a modern, web-based management console for managing Exchange Online." Want to manage mailboxes? EAC is where you go. Group management? Again, EAC. Microsoft explained: "The design of the EAC in Exchange Online aligns with the overall Microsoft 365 admin experience." Sadly, that alignment appears to extend to service wobbles caused by changes rolled out without due care and attention. Two hours after admitting things had gone awry, Microsoft said it was "continuing to test the rollback of the recent Exchange admin center (EAC) change while monitoring the results to determine if this resolves the impact." At this point, administrators were nodding sagely at an all-too familiar story. Of course rolling back the change did the trick. Microsoft stated as much in its final update: "A recent EAC configuration change resulted in unexpected HTTP responses within the affected request path, preventing admins from successfully accessing the EAC. "Reverting the identified change restored expected service functionality." Microsoft also assured customers it was reviewing the change to ensure it didn't make the same mistake again, as well as its monitoring and telemetry, to "improve detection and alerting for similar service behavior." The problem is that this is hardly a new phenomenon. In September, Microsoft made a configuration change that left some users unable to access SharePoint Online sites and pages. In April, another ill-thought-through change took down Outlook for iOS. And, in 2025, Microsoft 365 tumbled from the cloud because of yet another configuration change. It's almost as if testing changes consists of little more than asking Copilot, "does this look alright to you?" and then hitting the go button. The latest outage was resolved before the end of the working day, and a preliminary Post-Incident Report is due within two business days, with a final report due next week. Hopefully one or the other will contain words along the lines of "Hey, this keeps happening, maybe we should do some more testing before deploying to production?" ®

3f4c6d05dd16a54d: If you thought everyone was into chatbots, think again: about half of US adults never use the AI tools, and most have no interest in starting. According to Pew Research Center, older adults are the least likely to use chatbots, with roughly three-quarters of those aged 65 and older saying they never use them. That may be expected, yet more than half (58 percent) of adults aged 50 to 64 don't use them either. Those aged 18 to 29 use chatbots the most, at 66 percent, however even a third of them say they never do. About four in ten under 50 report not using them at all. Across all adults, 51 percent are chatbot refuseniks, so users are - just barely - the minority. Pew asked non-users to choose from five possible reasons. Six in ten cited simple lack of interest as a major factor, followed by the more familiar concerns of data privacy and the accuracy of chatbot answers. Some Reg readers might suspect older people avoid chatbots because they lack tech-savviness, but fewer than a third cited not knowing how to use them as a major reason. The authors of the survey also found fewer than one in five worried about what others might think of them for using the technology, so social stigma isn’t the deterrent either. Adoption also differs by race and ethnicity: non-users are more likely to be white, black or hispanic than Asian, according to Pew’s survey. The AI dodgers don't look ready to budge. Two-thirds (67 percent) say they’re unlikely to use the technology in the next 12 months, including 40 percent who say they’re not at all likely to change their mind. Another 12 percent are unsure, and just 5 percent of non-users think they'll probably try a chatbot over the next year. Perhaps abstainers were put off by a bad experience, such as Microsoft’s notorious racist chatbot Tay a decade ago. Or something more recent, like the Trump administration’s official America.gov service, which at the time of writing still displays a hotdog if you type that into the prompt. ®

f046a994d6828ccc: What is DNS? That's right, it's a database. You can disagree with me but you would be wrong. What can you put in a database? Strings, ints (and you learn the difference right quick if your AWS account ID has a leading zero!), JSON objects, coordinates; some of the databases out there have some pretty esoteric types. PostgreSQL supports circle, a polygon, a macaddr8, and a tsquery. Oracle will store a ROWID and your dignity. In a word, databases store data. Can you put answers in a database? Well sure; you could record that "3 + 2 is equal to 5" and store that answer. You can do the same with comparison operators; "3 is larger than 2" and so on. Take it a step further and you've built something with your database: a remarkably inconvenient calculator. So now we've established that you can store arithmetic and decisions in a database. And what can we do with those things? That's right, we can follow instructions! Good job! And what does following instructions require? Generally, memory; a place to store your numbers, your instructions, and which instruction comes next. If only we had a place to store those things. Oh right, we do; we have a database! Now connect those lookups together. Read an instruction, look up an answer, save the result, repeat as needed. So what have we built? That's right: a computer! And what can a computer run? Programs! My, you're quite good at this. And now, gentle reader: what program do we apparently have a moral obligation to run on every computer? Oh yes, though many of you are going to sit back and instead say "oh no" as the horror courses through you. I am talking about Doom. This very publication agrees with me! What have I done? That's right; I have compiled Doom for a 32-bit machine whose arithmetic and memory live in DNS. A small program supplies the wiring and the clock, neither of which the architects of DNS saw fit to include. But DNS does supply the answers. So, can we play Doom? Only if it's turn-based. It won't render on human timescales anyway. In my first attempt, I pressed Right, and then waited for 577 seconds to find out what happened. By using native transport, pipelining, packing registers densely, and optimizing instruction blocks, I was able to drop that to 146 seconds, before I hit a wall. BIND answers in about 7 µs per query over TCP and 4 µs over UDP, which is fast. The problem is that a 32-bit add is four DNS lookups, a branch is five, and a frame needs 6.6 million of them, so don't use a server that charges per request. And what do we do when BIND isn't performing the way we want it to? I don't know what you do, but I publish my code, then reach out to Paul Vixie, DNS pioneer and architect of BIND 8 to unjustifiably complain. Paul then apparently congratulates me on "the best use of RFC 2136 DNS UPDATE" that he'd ever seen. Given that he's a co-author of that RFC, I suspect he's seen a lot! Which was gratifying, but unhelpful. So let's take another crack at it. What if I do lookaheads? Good thought, bad outcome, because BIND is bound by message count, not chain depth. Well okay, I have some more tricks in my Big Bag of Stupid Ideas. So I went a bit further and via committing registers to DNS less often, moving lookups to UDP, telling BIND to stop padding answers with authority records, and requiring fewer lookups per instruction, I was ultimately able to get that press-right time down from 577 seconds to 146.3 seconds to 54.4 seconds, for a 10.6x improvement. And now I think I have hit a wall. Even at one DNS exchange per instruction (which is far better than anything realistically achievable), 1.4 million instructions at roughly 10 µs each is 14 seconds per tick. Doom says its tic rate is 35 per second, so "playable" is a tic every 28.6 ms. I remain at 54,000 ms, which is three orders of magnitude away from victory. Okay seriously, WHAT? This legitimately works. Every commit is an RFC 2136 UPDATE with a hard requirement: it fails unless the previous state is still exactly what was last written. Apparently "real" database people call that optimistic concurrency, or compare-and-swap. Joke's on you, friends; DNS has shipped with that since 1997; has your inferior database? The database itself is 6.4 million rows of truth tables. ff.01.0.add holds "001": 255 plus 1 is 00 carry 1. DNS is just acting as a librarian here, fetching memorized answers to any arithmetic question in-scope and returning the answer upon request. It's also verifiable! The frame that's spat out is checked on every pixel against an independent emulator. If one record is corrupted in the AND table, the answer changes, which proves there's no local fallback doing arithmetic for us. I've included tooling so that reviewers can run two commands against that repo and verify correctness. I also confess I cheated slightly here; the run I'm pulling these numbers from started from a checkpoint prepared by a normal emulator. It turns out that for SOME UNKNOWN REASON getting a cold boot through Doom's startup screens via DNS would take hours. Also, before the timer starts, DNS has to load those 6.4 million records, so it's a computer that takes roughly a minute to boot before it can even start. We can't cheat This runs atop nothing special: Debian's stock BIND 9.20, configured through named.conf. It lives in a container with networking disabled. I want to be very clear here: this isn't DNS pretending to be a CPU. The instruction decoding is done ahead of time by a compiler; BIND never executes an instruction itself. All that it sees is a key-value read, a conditional write, and 6.4 million rows of precomputed answers. So instead, think of this monstrosity as a database with a key-value read, a conditional write, and 6.4 million rows of precomputed answers. It's not really a computer; it's simply a very good database. And that turns out to be enough. ®
de69746aabbc012a: For over a decade now, the only "official" way to play Hideo Kojima's cult classic, P.T.—the long-discontinued "playable trailer" for Kojima's canceled "Silent Hills" project—has been via one of the increasingly rare PlayStation 4s that previously downloaded a copy during its monthslong availability window. Now, though, one coder is helping to preserve the game with a porting tool that builds a playable x86 PC executable from the original PS4 files.

Coder Lorean Xavier said he was inspired to work on the "P.T. for PC" project "because P.T. deserved to keep existing somewhere other than on consoles that still have it installed." The open source porting effort rebuilds the P.T. engine in C++ and Vulkan, using the original files from the PS4 game to re-create "every level, model, texture, sound, script and cutscene," according to its GitHub listing. That means players without their own legitimate decrypted copy of the original P.T. will have to track one down in order to generate a playable PC version.

The reliance on real P.T. files makes this port more authentic than previous hobbyist efforts to re-create the look and feel of P.T. for a PC audience. And while PS4 emulators recently reached a point where they could run P.T. completely, this native port also sports extra features, like upscaling and frame-generation, a camera mode, experimental third-person and VR support, and a "museum" section where you can look at and listen to in-game assets (including "unused content").
b865794ab8dffb03: AMD is expanding its rack-scale AI lineup with a design to run AI agents, offering CPU-only configurations or integrated CPU/GPU deployments, and liquid-cooled or air-cooled versions. Revealed at the Open Compute Project (OCP) Summit 2026 in San Jose, California, the chipmaker's new rack reference design is named Helion, while its existing system carries the moniker Helios, which we can't help feeling is inviting confusion a little. Helion offers an OCP-compliant blueprint for agentic AI infrastructure built around AMD's CPUs and accelerators. AMD launched Helios earlier this year for frontier-scale AI training and large-scale inference. Helion's enterprise configuration instead combines agent execution and inference within a single rack. Customers can opt for a CPU-only hyperscale configuration or an enterprise configuration with a mix of CPU and GPU blades. Depending on configuration, AMD advertises up to 32,768 of AMD's "Zen 6" CPU cores, delivered via compute nodes fitted with 256-core versions of its Venice Epyc processor, up to 16 of its Instinct MI350P GPU accelerators, and up to 102 Tbps of networking bandwidth. The CPU-only hyperscale version offers dedicated capacity for agent execution and connections to separate model inference infrastructure, while the enterprise configuration combines agent execution, GPU inference, and supporting workloads in one rack. Both configurations offer dense, balanced, or high-performance CPU blades. For dense deployments, EPYC 9006 chips rated at 400 W are used, while performance blades sport a version of the chip with just 96 cores but clocked at 5 GHz. Balanced blades use 256-core processors rated at 600 W. There are also GPU inference blades, with eight Instinct MI350P GPUs in a 5U server, plus general-purpose blades, intended for database and storage servers or technical compute workloads. AMD SVP for Compute and Enterprise AI Dan McNamara said agentic AI is not a single workload, spanning enterprise applications and complex workflows, each with different compute requirements. "To do that takes optimized compute and infrastructure that can adapt to different workloads. With AMD Helion, we are bringing Epyc performance, open software and flexible rack designs together so our partners can build systems around customer needs and make efficient use of available power," he added. AMD says it plans to contribute the Helion specifications to OCP, making them available to the community for further development and adoption. Partner-built Helion configurations are scheduled for November 2026. In its announcement, AMD cites Cisco, Dell, HPE, Foxconn, Lenovo, Supermicro, and others as on board with the new kit. ®

a28af2371faff12a: Microsoft has closed a loophole that let users sidestep the need for an account during setup for consumer versions of Windows 11. If users clicked "Learn More" when the setup process prompted for a Microsoft account, the Out-of-Box Experience (OOBE) skipped directly to the point where they just had to enter a name and password. Windows prodder "Bob Pony," who first documented the loophole, reported its removal. We tried the original trick on real Intel hardware and found it was possible to skip the Microsoft account requirement by clicking a link, but no longer. Other hacks – for those who dare to use unofficial Windows setup routes – still exist, though they are beyond the skill set of the average user. Microsoft requires an account during initial setup of Windows 11 Home and Pro for personal use. For consumers, using Windows 11 without an account can be tricky because services such as OneDrive require authentication. Microsoft is far from the only operating system vendor to demand an account during setup, but many Linux distributions, by contrast, don't require one. According to Bob Pony, the loophole was "quietly patched server side," which makes sense. Microsoft was hardly likely to leave it flapping open for long. Microsoft has won this round of account workaround Whac-a-Mole, though another bypass may yet pop up. ®
c51c6bb06fc006e1: Formula 1’s lengthy 2026 season is entering its final stretch. The sport took to the floodlit streets of Singapore on Sunday night, but Saturday saw action, too; this Grand Prix weekend was also the final of six sprints this year. The night race might be one of modern F1’s greatest spectacles. From overhead shots, the track becomes a bright, illuminated ribbon among the looming darkness of the city-state’s overpasses and skyscrapers. At ground level, the cars shower glittering sparks from their titanium skid blocks as the drivers flirt with how close they can get to the walls. As tracks go, the 90-degree turns and concrete barrier-lined streets were a world away from the abrasive tarmac and ample runoff of Malaysia last time out. But the tropical heat and humidity were a constant given both locations’ proximity to the equator.

In Malaysia (which was still technically the Bahrain GP), a pre-race downpour disrupted things mightily. On Saturday morning in Singapore, shortly before the start of the sprint, it seemed history was about to rhyme when the skies opened. With standing water in places on the track, the sprint was delayed by 30 minutes. The sprint format, where a short extra race replaces a practice session a day before the main event, is unloved by the drivers and teams. For one thing, there’s little prestige in winning Saturday’s sprint. And with qualifying just a few hours later, risk-taking is discouraged lest one wreck the car and ruin Sunday’s race a day early.

Oh no, not again! Credit: Mark Thompson/Getty Images And in Singapore, like most street circuits, the proximity of the unyielding barriers that line the track means there are real, punishing consequences for getting it even a little wrong.

c25f6308f79c3ce0: Yandex engineers are working to restore services after Ukraine launched drone strikes on three of its five Russian datacenters. The strikes began overnight on October 7-8, "seriously damaging" Yandex's Sasovo datacenter and leading to a total shutdown. Ukrainian drones struck again on the morning of October 9, targeting the company's Kaluga datacenter, resulting in part of its infrastructure being taken offline. Dima Pirogov, head of Yandex's fintech division, confirmed via Telegram on Sunday morning that a third strike targeted the company's Vladimir site, which supports Yandex Pay. A day later, services remain offline, although Pirogov said users' money is safe. "I'm very sorry I can't tell you yet that everything is working again," the exec wrote. "The team continues to restore services and is checking every step. When it comes to your money, it's important to us not just to restore Yandex Pay as quickly as possible, but also to ensure that everything is working reliably. "I understand that you're not waiting for words, but for access to your money. And I understand how hard it is to wait when you can't use it. We can't give you a precise timeline for the restoration yet, but we promise: we won't stop until the service is back online." Yandex Pay is the company's digital payments service. Users can make online and in-store purchases, pay in installments, and split bills with friends and family. It's also integrated into online shopping experiences. It is comparable to Apple Pay or Google Pay, while Yandex more broadly offers services similar to Google's. Yandex said engineers are prioritizing the most-used services, and reported that access to the Alice AI assistant, Mail, Maps, Search, and Taxi is being restored, but other features remain offline. The company's status page lists widespread outages across Yandex Cloud, its public cloud platform, following the attacks. Updates from the maintenance team describe partial availability despite the outage indicators. They suggest that some customers may be able to access certain features, such as Yandex Cloud Console and API, but availability remains inconsistent across the platform. In its most recent update, the company said: "The Yandex Cloud platform is still operating in a limited mode. Our specialists continue restoration work around the clock. The technical support team receives an increased number of requests, so the response time can be increased. "Our recommendations continue to be relevant. We recommend using alternative sites for hosting and reserving resources." Internet monitoring organization Netblocks reported that Yandex Cloud's network connectivity was at 30 percent of normal levels on October 11. Ukraine president Volodymyr Zelensky said the drone attacks were a response to Russia's own, which had targeted datacenters in Kyiv. The BBC reported that in September, Russian drone strikes targeted a business center in the capital city, killing four people and damaging a datacenter, which in turn resulted in around 100,000 households losing internet access. The attacks led to other knock-on effects, such as public transport boards not displaying information in Lutsk. Kyiv's attack on the Vladimir site on Sunday morning came hours after controversial comments from US president Donald Trump, who accused Zelensky of wanting "to make problems for the world" by continuing to attack Russian oil refineries. Trump went on to say that it was time for Ukraine to elect a new president after Zelensky said measures should not be taken that allow Russia to generate more revenue to fund its war. Zelensky was referring to a deal between Trump and Putin to release diesel from Russia to the US and the rest of the world. Later that day, the US president claimed Russia and Ukraine had agreed to an "energy ceasefire" to halt attacks on each other's energy infrastructure. Kyiv said it was unaware of the agreement before Trump announced it on his social media platform, but was willing to halt attacks on Russian energy infrastructure if Moscow reciprocated. Russia launched a missile attack on a Ukrainian power plant hours later. ®

273a91b33201d9e7: UCLA and Oracle have settled a dispute over a troubled ERP project originally budgeted at $120 million, with the vendor waiving $1.31 million in outstanding fees and granting $3.1 million in credits against future charges. In May, the University of California's Compliance and Audit Committee recommended a settlement [PDF] of UCLA's pre-litigation dispute with Oracle, which the Board of Regents approved. According to documents released in response to a California Public Records Act request, UCLA stopped paying its Oracle subscription in September 2024 over what it described as shortcomings in grants management functionality. UCLA and Oracle signed their first agreement relating to the project – called Ascend – in November 2017. The project had a revised go-live date of January 2025, but was paused in mid-2024. The settlement records UCLA's allegation that "the ERP Cloud Services did not perform as warranted in the Oracle Agreement." "The ERP Cloud Services lacked sufficient functionality to meet the University's requirements and could not be used by the University as expected," said the document, which was seen by The Register. It continued that "the University incurred costs and delays due to the ERP Cloud Services inability to meet the University's requirements." It added: "As a result, Oracle breached the Oracle Agreement." Under the settlement, UCLA agreed to pay Oracle $350,000 of the $1.66 million in outstanding invoices. Oracle then waived the remaining balance – $1.31 million – and credited $3.1 million against future Oracle fees. These credits expire at the end of May 2028. The agreement says the university should not make public statements about its terms, which are to remain confidential, although both parties acknowledged that UCLA is subject to the California Public Records Act. The Register has asked Oracle to comment. The settlement was obtained by California resident Eric Guyer, founder of independent Oracle cost consultancy Advizant. In a social media post, he said that the credits suggested UCLA would continue with the project in some form, with Oracle as the main vendor. Guyer suggested Oracle most likely discounted its software to win the "coveted" UCLA logo. He estimated the total subscription value at around $12 million over ten years. He said Oracle tends to move decisively when unpaid bills on clear contractual terms back it into a corner. "This is rare despite the lore of its litigious nature. Everyone has a line. In any case, UCLA's claim probably went to Oracle because it was the easiest to point a finger at: consultants sell effort, not outcomes, and internal staff can only be fired." However, he said the average customer should not conclude that claiming a breach and stopping payment is advisable. "It can be effective, but is an exceedingly painful path," he claimed. "In this rare case, Oracle agreed to eat some shit at the end of a poorly planned implementation in exchange for UCLA's silence in the fiercely competitive higher ed market. In other public implementation fights, Oracle struck first or countersued, with press releases to match." UCLA serves around 49,000 students and manages a budget of around $11 billion. A 2025 report [PDF] presented to the University of California Board of Regents' Finance and Capital Strategies Committee said that among the "Top Issues, Risks and Challenges" the UCLA project leadership faced was "Oracle's lack of responsiveness – particularly regarding licensing costs and support." It added that the project's original $120 million budget was revised down to $98.9 million, with $13.5 million remaining as of December 31, 2024. The report, covering the period through December 2024, said the project started in April 2018 and was originally expected to end in July 2020. The document described it as a "comprehensive business transformation initiative" to modernize the university's financial, budgetary, and research administration operations by moving to Oracle Cloud SaaS. It also included retrofitting any systems that connected with the main finance system. The procurement module, BruinBuy Plus, went live in January 2024, but the main "Oracle Financials go-live has been paused since August 2 [2024] and is undergoing program assessment," the document said. Among the mitigation plans in the review was to "finalize the decision on whether to continue with the current vendor or explore alternatives" based on a reassessment of the tool and provider. According to the settlement document, the University told Oracle via email on June 20, 2025 that the "University wanted to terminate the Ascend project and the ERP Cloud Services." In May, a spokesperson for UCLA said in a statement to The Register: "The University continues to evaluate the most effective path forward for financial systems modernization." Under the terms of the settlement agreement, the University and Oracle have agreed to make no further claims for damages related to the contract dispute, and neither has admitted liability. According to a report from campus newspaper Daily Bruin, UCLA was still using legacy financial systems software designed in the 1980s when the budget was just seven percent of its current size. It was a mainframe-based "ancient relic of a system," former project steering committee member Reem Hanna-Harwell told the newspaper. The Daily Bruin reported that at least $213 million had been spent and cited a May 2024 town hall presentation projecting total costs of roughly $286 million. ®

db958e2353fb73d9: No organization in the world operates more robots than Amazon. The company already has more than 1 million robots working in warehouses around the clock to make tens of millions of same-day and one-day package deliveries happen on a daily basis—and Amazon is poised to significantly grow that robotic fleet in the coming years as it establishes new factories to churn out increasingly more capable robot workers.

Despite deploying so many robots, Amazon is also the second-largest corporate employer in the world, with more than 1.5 million full-time and part-time human workers, according to its 2025 annual report. Amazon executives say that the growing robot fleet has eased the burden on its human workforce by taking on the toughest fulfillment center tasks that carry the greatest risks of physical fatigue and injury. But labor advocacy groups and independent researchers point to evidence suggesting that warehouse automation driven by AI is not all upside for the humans who work alongside robots.

“For the last 100 years, most of the automation that we've seen usually happens away from workers—you're taking that high-risk task away from the worker, and you're doing so in a way that is not physically proximate,” Brian Greenwood, professor of business at George Mason University, told Ars. “The rise of collaborative robots really changes that dynamic for two reasons: one is that it is physically proximate, and two, the robot has the ability to dictate the pace of work.”
3ef54f5cc0b953b9: Not satisfied with shoehorning Copilot into every crevice of Office, Microsoft is adding Office to the Copilot app, while also evicting the AI assistant from certain parts of Outlook. The plan is simple: give the Copilot app a prompt, and it will create an Office document (for example, Word) and let a user edit it in the appropriate Office application while keeping the Copilot conversation going. The document can be shared with other users too, who can use the prompt Copilot to tweak it. Albeit an interesting approach, we suspect the system's reliance on OneDrive, rather than that enterprise favorite, SharePoint, might put off some customers. The new feature is also only rolling out to Frontier customers in Chat and Cowork. There's also a question-mark over Microsoft's commitment. The company is quick to drop or deprecate technology when its attention drifts elsewhere. The ability to create a theme in Outlook with Copilot is an example. Less than two years ago, Microsoft announced "Themes by Copilot in Outlook" which, according to the software and cloud biz, marked "the first instance of dynamic AI-generated theming in productivity applications." Themes by Copilot in Outlook, for users with a Copilot license, was a relatively simple piece of technology and could be dynamic, showing imagery inspired by the user's locale (if location permissions were enabled) and updating at regular intervals, for example, based on the current weather. It was all terribly exciting, and Microsoft imagined a world where users might fiddle with their productivity applications in the same way that "you might accent your desk with a candle or photos, spruce up your office with artwork or plants." After all, what's better than watching a beautiful sunset while Outlook quietly explodes in the background? However, after less than two years, the feature is for the chop, according to a post in Microsoft's Message Center. "Themes by Copilot," it wrote at the weekend, "will be removed from Settings, and users will no longer be able to select or return to a Theme by Copilot after changing to a different theme." If you're currently using a Theme by Copilot, it won't go anywhere until you change it, but after that, there's no going back. It's unclear why Microsoft is retiring the feature so soon after announcing it. It might be due to low usage (we can imagine some administrators weren't happy that users could override the selected appearance of their tools) or a step back from the Copilot All The Things approach Microsoft has taken in recent years. It is, however, a salutary warning for anyone enthusiastically embracing Office in Copilot, an interesting feature that will make for some impressive keynotes. It will also need to demonstrate its worth or face the same fate as Themes by Copilot when Microsoft moves on to The Next Big Thing. ®
3a228466c214dfd8: London's minicab drivers want Mayor Sadiq Khan to put the brakes on robotaxis before they threaten thousands of jobs, with a new City Hall report casting doubt on whether the capital is ready for driverless cars. The Independent Workers' Union of Great Britain (IWGB) has called on Transport for London (TfL) to halt the rollout following the publication of a London Assembly Transport Committee report on Monday. The 66-page report makes uncomfortable reading for the companies hoping to unleash fleets of driverless taxis on London's streets. "As it stands, we currently have not heard sufficient evidence to persuade us that London should welcome autonomous passenger services," it concludes. Google's Waymo, British startup Wayve, and Chinese tech giant Baidu are among those gearing up to bring autonomous passenger services to London. Waymo has already been testing its cars in the capital and hopes to launch a commercial fleet of "low hundreds" this year, subject to regulatory approval. Uber and Wayve have secured TfL private hire licenses for vehicles offering supervised self-driving rides, meaning a human driver remains legally in control, and Freenow and Baidu are targeting a fully driverless launch in 2027. London has around 105,000 licensed private hire drivers, many of whom have reason to worry about cars that can do their jobs without them. "Every car feeds a family, and the prospect of not being able to earn money leaves us all with a deep uncertainty as to how we will provide for them. We already struggle to get by as it is," said Gholomreza "Rez" Kamyabi, an Uber driver and vice chair of the IWGB Private Hire Drivers union. The committee heard warnings that robotaxis could put large numbers of drivers out of work, and wants TfL to work with unions and operators to retrain, redeploy, and fund those affected. The IWGB, however, wants the rollout stopped. "The IWGB Private Hire Drivers Union opposes the rollout of driverless cars," said union president Alex Marshall, warning the technology could put thousands out of work while benefiting tech companies and investors. Jobs aren't the only concern. Under the government's interim Automated Passenger Services permitting scheme, the Driver and Vehicle Standards Agency (DVSA) issues operating permits. TfL must consent before a service launches in London, but cannot independently suspend or revoke a permit once issued. TfL also has no formal say over existing driverless trials, and operators aren't legally required to report incidents to it, although some have shared information voluntarily. The report details several incidents involving autonomous test vehicles, including a car reportedly entering a police crime scene cordon in April, another filmed turning the wrong way into a one-way street in June, and a reported collision with a motorcycle in July. It also questions how robotaxis would handle medical emergencies, passenger safety, and accessibility. None of the autonomous vehicles currently being trialed are wheelchair accessible. Then there's congestion. Robotaxis could lure passengers away from public transportation while adding more traffic as vehicles travel empty between fares. The committee wants operators to report their empty mileage so TfL can assess the impact. Londoners aren't exactly clamoring for the technology either. A YouGov survey commissioned by the committee found that 42 percent opposed autonomous passenger vehicles, compared with 29 percent who supported them. Just 29 percent said they would be likely to use one. The committee stopped short of calling for a ban, instead recommending tougher safety requirements, giving TfL powers to cap vehicle numbers, and a process to request the immediate suspension of permits. It also wants TfL to take over permitting when the Automated Vehicles Act is fully implemented, expected in the second half of 2027. At the time of the investigation, TfL had not yet published the criteria it would use to approve driverless passenger services. So London is preparing for robotaxis while its transport authority works out the rules, Assembly members question the benefits, and cab drivers demand the whole thing be stopped. Still, at least the cars won't complain about their working conditions.®
4c9ebb897b3f0f40: This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.
Mars may be a hellhole, but the moon is not far behind
The US and China are racing to build bases on the moon, with NASA hoping to establish a small lunar city by the end of the century. But the moon is a tremendously hostile place to set up camp.

A sprawling lunar base must be safe for its inhabitants, protected from falling asteroids, endless cosmic radiation, razor-sharp lunar dust, and torturous temperature swings. It also must be somewhat self-sustaining.
That will require autonomous robots, nuclear power, and a way to use the moon’s resources to keep the base operating. But the chief obstacle may be one of political will.
Find out what stands in the way of a city on the moon.
—Robin George Andrews

4716b75a3ed74c46: A piece of internet history that once traveled strapped to a pigeon's leg is up for auction at Christie's, where someone has already bid $4,000 for what might be the world's most expensive ping. The unusual lot is a surviving IP packet from a 2001 experiment in which Norwegian Linux enthusiasts decided to find out whether the internet could, in fact, run on birds. The idea dates back to April 1, 1990, when American network engineer David Waitzman published RFC 1149, titled A Standard for the Transmission of IP Datagrams on Avian Carriers. Written in the wonderfully dry language of an official internet standards document, the April Fools' proposal outlined how carrier pigeons could transport IP datagrams between locations. It noted that avian carriers could provide high bandwidth, although latency would be another matter entirely. Most people appreciated the joke and moved on. The Bergen Linux User Group (BLUG), however, decided to actually build the thing. On April 28, 2001, the group put RFC 1149 to the test using racing pigeons, printers, and scanners. IP packets were printed as hexadecimal strings on strips of paper, attached to the birds' legs, and flown between two lofts 5km (roughly 3 miles) apart. The results hardly amounted to a ringing endorsement of pigeon-powered networking. Nine packets were dispatched, but only four replies came back, giving the experiment a packet-loss rate of about 56 percent. Still, the network worked, at least in the loosest possible sense of the word. Actual IP packets had traveled through the air without a single router, fiber-optic cable, or telecoms provider getting involved. One of those packets has now resurfaced at auction house Christie's as part of its Fine Printed Books & Manuscripts Including Americana and Science auction. The item is a small scroll of paper measuring just 41mm by 210mm, complete with creases from being rolled up and attached to the pigeon's leg. It is now framed, with an inscription on the reverse identifying it as the property of Waitzman, to whom it was presented in 2002. Christie's initially estimated the packet would fetch between $2,000 and $3,000, but bidding has already reached $4,000. The auction closes on October 13. The auction house describes the experiment as an example of the internet's tradition of the "artful hack," celebrating the technical ingenuity and sense of humor of its early community. There is, of course, something rather fitting about an internet packet that took to the skies 25 years ago now commanding thousands of dollars. Most packets disappear into the ether once they've served their purpose. This one ended up in a frame and is being sold by Christie's. Not bad for something delivered by a pigeon. ®
